answer:
**The best notification may be no notification.** A user likely to open a message may already have been about to return to the app. Sending them a notification could produce an impressive open rate with little incremental benefit, while increasing fatigue. The decision is about the difference between sending and not sending.

**Use a simple comparison.** User A returns with probability 0.80 without a notification and 0.82 with one: estimated lift is 0.02. User B returns with probability 0.30 without and 0.40 with: lift is 0.10. A prediction model optimizing only return probability may prefer A; a causal policy may prefer B, after considering costs and harms. [3](https://miguelhernan.org/whatifbook)

**Separate eligibility from optimization.** Consent, quiet hours, frequency caps, stale events, and duplicate suppression should be enforced before deciding which eligible message is best. A high predicted reward should not override a hard no-contact rule. Scheduling and delivery need idempotent keys so retries do not create repeated pushes.

Use randomized no-send holdouts where appropriate to measure incrementality. Track delayed retention, opt-outs, uninstalls, and complaint rates rather than rewarding immediate clicks alone. Multiple campaigns can compete for the same attention budget, so evaluating each in isolation may miss combined fatigue.

When context or delivery state is missing, use an explicit conservative fallback. Monitor by user cohort and message type, because an aggregate positive effect can conceal a group receiving too many irrelevant interruptions. A causal score is an estimate with uncertainty, not a directly observed fact about what one specific user would have done otherwise.

**Technical details and references.**

Treat “send nothing” as an explicit action. Estimate incremental long-term benefit of a notification relative to no notification, conditioned on user context, message type, prior contact frequency, and local time. High open probability alone can select users who would return anyway.

Enforce quiet hours, consent, deduplication, channel limits, and per-user frequency caps before optimization. Choose send time with a contextual policy or hazard model, and use a durable scheduler with idempotent delivery keys. A model retry must not produce duplicate pushes. Keep suppression fast when the underlying event becomes stale or the user has already acted.

Randomize holdouts to measure causal retention lift and negative outcomes such as opt-outs and uninstalls. Delayed reward means the policy cannot be judged by immediate clicks alone. Account for interference between multiple campaigns competing for the same attention budget. Monitor subgroup fatigue and delivery failures; when features are missing, conservative suppression is often preferable to an aggressive generic notification.

**Mathematical and practical explanation.** The relevant quantity is incremental value $\mathbb E[Y(1)-Y(0)|X]$ minus notification cost, not simply $P(open|send,X)$. Maintain randomized no-send controls where appropriate and include fatigue/opt-out outcomes. A user who would return anyway can have high open probability and near-zero incremental benefit, illustrating why predictive propensity and causal uplift differ. [3](https://miguelhernan.org/whatifbook)

For the implementation or system context discussed above, see [1](https://engineering.fb.com/2022/10/31/ml-applications/instagram-notification-management-machine-learning/) and [2](https://www.linkedin.com/blog/engineering/member-customer-experience/bringing-project-every-member-to-life).
